problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 12 \\ -12 & -9\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}18 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} & -\frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A,$ $Σ,$ and $V$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the second column of $U?$

examples.knowledge_point: Determining the Columns of the First Matrix Given Part of a Singular Value Decomposition
examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14094923/assets/ea3e5c13d236a733350a1d23b8629cd481f9316e16ab7558873e305fe198eb98.png)
Consider the matrices $A,$ $\Sigma,$ and $V$ shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the second column of $U?$
examples.worked_solution:
Recall that if $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ and $\sigma_i \neq 0,$ then the $i$th column of $U$ can be found as

$$
\mathbf{u}_i = \dfrac{1}{\sigma_i} A\mathbf{v}_i,
$$

 

where $\mathbf v_i$ is the $i$th column of the matrix $V.$

From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that the singular values are $\sigma_1=9$ and $\sigma_2=4.$ Therefore, the second column of $U$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}6 & -5 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{12}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 12 \\ 12 & -4\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}13 & 0 \\ 0 & 12\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}{v}_{11} & {v}_{12} \\ {v}_{21} & {v}_{22}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the value of $|{v}_{11}|+|{v}_{21}|?$
feedback.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ the columns of $V$ must be the right singular vectors of $A,$ i.e., the unit eigenvectors of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that the singular values are ${\sigma }_{1}=13$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=12.$ So, the first column of $V$ corresponds to the singular value ${\sigma }_{1}=13.$

Hence, we need to find a unit eigenvector of ${A}^{T}\,A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=169.$ 

- Computing ${A}^{T}\,A,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 12 \\ 12 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}3 & 12 \\ 12 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 12 \\ 12 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 12 \\ 12 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}153 & -12 \\ -12 & 160\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Computing ${A}^{T}\,A-169I,$ we get

$$
{A}^{T}\,A-169I=[\begin{aligned}153 & -12 \\ -12 & 160\end{aligned}]-169[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-16 & -12 \\ -12 & -9\end{aligned}]
$$

- Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-169I)v=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we get 

$$
\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore,

$$
|{v}_{11}|+|{v}_{21}|=|-\frac{3}{5}|+|\frac{4}{5}|=\frac{7}{5}.
$$
